title: A comparison with another grammar guide (part 2): the copula
summary: The second commentary looks at how the copula だ and です are treated, and why the course keeps them as one logical element.

blocks.text: This is the second commentary episode. Last time the subject was が; this time it is the copula. The course argues that a model which makes だ a vague declarative marker takes away one of the pillars of Japanese structure.

A logical Japanese sentence can end in only three ways: with a **verb**, with an **adjective**, or with a **noun plus the copula**. A bare noun is not an engine. On one side stand verbs, adjectives and the copula; on the other nouns, particles and conjunctions. The copula always attaches to a noun and says that A is B, one way: さくらは日本人だ means Sakura belongs to the set of Japanese people, not the reverse.

In casual speech だ and particles are often dropped, just as English drops words in "Got up early this morning." That does not mean they are unnecessary: dropping is a legal shortcut because the listener can fill the gap. The course also treats だ and です as the same copula, with です being slightly eccentric in one respect.

blocks.en: Sakura, Japanese. (casual, だ and は dropped)

items: Three ways to end a logical sentence: verb, adjective, noun + copula.
The copula is a one-way equals sign.
In casual speech だ can be dropped, but it is still understood.
